newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela urges Chiluba to delay Nov 18 Zambian poll.
newsitem.headline: Mandela urges Chiluba to delay Nov 18 Zambian poll.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela on Thursday urged Zambian leader Frederick Chiluba to delay the country's general elections scheduled for next week.

"This morning I sent an urgent fax (recommending to Chiluba) that he must...postpone the elections in the interests of peace in the country," Mandela told a news conference in the port city of Durban.

Mandela said Chiluba had two options, either to postpone the elections or declare a state of emergency in the southern African country which would result in an automatic postponement of the elections due on November 18.

"President Chiluba can take one of two options to do this. One is to declare a state of emergency which would automatically postpone the elections and the second, it is his prerogative in terms of the law to postpone the elections," he said.

Judge Richard Goldstone, who has served as prosecutor in the war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and is now a South African Constitutional Court judge, travelled to Lusaka this week to meet Zambian Electoral Commission chairman Bobby Bwalya.
Mandela said Goldstone was told by Bwalya that he had no powers in terms of the constitution to postpone the election.

Seven opposition parties, including former president Kenneth Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP), are boycotting the elections which they say have been arranged to ensure that Chiluba's Movement for Multi-party Democracy (MMD) remains in office.
The parties are opposed to a new constitution which bars some candidates, including Kaunda, from standing for president if they are first-generation Zambians.
Kaunda was head of state for nearly three decades, leading Zambia to independence from Britain and ruling until Chiluba defeated him in polls in 1991.

The Zambian president travelled to Pretoria on Tuesday for an hour-long meeting with Mandela, who afterwards said Chiluba had put forth a "very important" suggestion which could end an opposition party boycott of the elections but did not elaborate.

Rioting university students in Lusaka on Monday joined calls for Chiluba to reopen dialogue with his political opponents and possibly suspend polls until all parties reach consensus on the rules governing the elections.

Western governments, many sharing opposition concerns, have cut or frozen aid to Zambia in an attempt to persuade the Zambian government to reverse contentious constitutional clauses and reopen voter registration.
The Chiluba government has repeatedly stated it will not be dictated to by foreign governments.
